title: Hearing inward
hookLine: Avalokiteshvara's practice of turning hearing back to its source (Surangama)

lines: A SOUND IS GOING ON RIGHT NOW.
THE ONE WHO HEARS THE WORLD.
cards: Somewhere near you, a sound is going on right now. A fan, a car passing, a voice in another room. It arrived without being asked.
Ears don't have lids. Now a stranger question: what is it that hears the sound? Not the sound, and not quite the ear.
The hearing. In a Mahayana sutra called the Surangama, a bodhisattva says his whole path opened when he turned that question around. He is Avalokiteshvara, the one who hears the cries of the world.

teach.h: HOW DID EACH OF YOU BREAK THROUGH?
teach.b: In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha puts a plain question to a gathering of awakened beings: how did each of you break through? The answers differ. One woke through sight.
One through a fragrance drifting in the air. One through the feel of bath water on the skin. Avalokiteshvara answers: through hearing.

Then, instead of following each sound outward, he turned the hearing back toward its source. One English rendering of the sutra's phrase is entering the stream and forgetting the place. Sounds kept coming and going.
Then even the coming and going fell quiet, sound and silence both, and still the hearing was there, untouched by either. It fits him.

In Chinese he is Guanyin, a name the tradition reads as the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In the sutra, the one who learned to listen to listening is the one who can answer every kind of being who calls.
After all the answers, the Buddha asks Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, which gate suits the people of this world.
Manjushri chooses the gate of the ear. His reasons, in paraphrase: hearing works in every direction at once, through walls, in the dark, with the eyes shut. It doesn't need anything to face.
And when a sound ends, the hearing doesn't end with it. The car passes. The street goes quiet.
Whatever was hearing the car is now hearing the quiet.

how: In Chinese Buddhism and in some Chan and Zen communities, Avalokiteshvara's practice of turning the hearing around is taught as a meditation method, and the passage from the Surangama Sutra is studied and recited.

o: silencing outside noise so you can focus
listening closely to your own inner thoughts
turning the hearing back toward its source

p: how did each of you break through?
hearing, turned back to its source

s: in the Surangama, every bodhisattva awakens through hearing
the answers differ: sight, a fragrance, bath water. hearing is Avalokiteshvara's way.
Manjushri picks the way of hearing for the people of this world
hearing reaches in every direction, through walls and in the dark.
in this practice, hearing stops when the sound stops
the sound goes; the hearing is still there, now hearing the quiet.

games.q: you're Manjushri. the Buddha has heard many ways of awakening and asks which one suits the people of this world. which do you choose?
games.why: Manjushri chooses Avalokiteshvara's gate, the ear: hearing works in every direction and doesn't end when a sound does.

practice: Let the eyes close or soften, and for a little while just listen: sounds near and far, loud and faint, without naming them.
Then gently turn around, and instead of reaching for the next sound, notice the listening itself, open and already here.
When a sound pulls you out, hear it and turn back, and in the gaps between sounds, notice that hearing is still on.

wordCard.voice: Hearing inward. In the Surangama Sutra, Avalokiteshvara's way: listening, then turning the hearing back toward its source. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the bodhisattva of compassion; in Chinese, Guanyin.

carryVoice: Your line: turn the hearing around. Any sound, a siren or a ringtone, can work like a bell. See you tomorrow.
